div.p: The object-oriented design methods and their CASE tools are widely used in practice by m a n y real-time software developers. However, object-oriented CASE tools require a n additional step of identifying tasks f r o m a given design model. Unfortunately, it is dificult t o automate this step for a couple of reasons: (1) there are inherent discrepancies between objects and tasks; and

(2) it is hard t o derive tasks while maximizing real-tame schedulability since this problem makes a non-trivial optimization problem. As a result, in practical objectoriented CASE tools, task identification is usually performed in a n ad-hoc manner using hints provided by human designers. I n this paper, we present a systematic, schedulability-aware approach that can help mapping real-time object-oriented models to multi-threaded implementations. I n our approach, a task contains a group of mutually exclusive transactions that m a y possess different periods and deadline. For this new task model, we provide a schedulability analysis algorithm. W e also show how the run-time system is implemented and how executable code is generated in our framework. W e have performed a case study. It shows the d i f i c d t y of task derivation problem and the utility of the automated synthesis of implemenation.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The object-oriented design methods and their CASE tools are widely used in practice in developing complex *The work reported in this paper is supported in part by MOST under the National Research Laboratory (NRL) grant 2000-N-NL-01-C-136 and by Automatic Control Research Center (ACRC).

real-time systems. However, object-oriented CASE tools require an additional step of identifying tasks from a given design model. Unfortunately, it is difficult to automate this step for a couple of reasons: (1) there are inherent discrepancies between objects and tasks; and ( 2 ) it is hard to derive tasks while maximizing real-time schedulability since this problem makes a non-trivial optimization problem. As a result, in practical object-oriented CASE tools, task identification is usually performed in an ad-hoc manner using hints provided by human designers. However, task derivation has a significant effect on the real-time schedulability of the resultant system.

Once task derivation is performed, the next step in object-oriented real-time system development is timing analysis. This can be done relatively easily using several scheduling algorithms in the literature [6, 51. Whereas commercial object-oriented CASE tools including UML-RT have not yet provided timing analysis features and timeliness guarantees, there have been several research results on automated implementation of ROOM-based designs and associated schedulability analyses [2, 9, 101. However, these approaches are applicable to a system design only after tasks are completely identified, and do not address the schedulability-aware mapping of real-time objectoriented models to implementations. Thus, real-time designers need rigorous methods for such mappings.

In commercial object-oriented CASE tools, it is a common practice to map each of individual objects to a single task [12] since this is simple and natural. The other extreme practice is to map all objects in a system to a single task. For example, both RoseRT for UML-RT [13] and ObjecTime Developer [7] for ROOM map all active objects (a capsule instance in the UML-RT terminology) into a single task. RoseRT allows designers to map capsule instances to multiple tasks.

Unfortunately, this requires that the UML-RT design be changed. Designers need to convert their original design model into a dynamically configurable system by associating capsule instances with dynamically created, optional tasks and then inserting code incarnating those capsule instances in initial state transitions of fixed capsule instances. This hurts one of the advantages of object-oriented design methods -separation of design models and implementations. Nevertheless, this approach is effective to reduce blocking time due to priority inversion.

In this paper, we present a systematic, schedulability-aware method that can automatically generate an implementation from object-oriented design model for a real-time system. We also show how the run-time system is implemented and how executable code is generated. To derive tasks from a design, we rely on the notion of a transaction. It denotes an end-to-end computation from an external input to an external output. It can be described as a sequence or chain of events flowing through the end-to-end computation. A transaction may be associated with timing constraints such as a period and a deadline as in [9]. Our approach groups mutually exclusive transactions into a task to reduce the number of tasks. As a result, a task may have multiple scheduling attributes including periods, execution times, and blocking times. Note that transactions in a task may have different periods and deadlines. We provide a new schedulability analysis algorithm that can take into account this task model. To further reduce the number of tasks, we also adopt preemption threshold scheduling presented in [15], and the notion of a non-preemptive group [ll, 121. The end result of our approach is an automated implementation method which maps a real-time object-oriented model to a multi-t hreaded implementation.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 overviews the UML-RT design model which becomes the source of our implementation model. Section 3 presents the details of our approach. Section 4 explains the inter-workings and implementation details of a CASE tool that supports our approach. Section 5 presents a simple example which demonstrates the application of our approach. We conclude this paper in Section 6.

div.head: UML-RT and its CASE Tool
div.p: In this section, we give an overview of UML-RT and RoseRT since UML-RT is used as a source programming language in our approach and RoseRT is the CASE tool of our choice.

div.head: Overview of UML-RT
div.p: The UML (Unified Modeling Language) is a graphical language for specifying, visualizing, constructing, documenting, and executing software systems. It represents a collection of the best engineering practices that have proven successful in modeling of large and complex systems. This has become de facto industrial standards as a modeling language and the most recent documentation was made in June, 1999 as version

Rational Software [13] developed UML-RT ('UML Real-Time), which is not yet included in the standard UML 1.3 by OMG. It has been developed to address a category of systems that are characterized as complex, event-driven, and potentially distributed. A set of new modeling constructs has been added to the UML syntax. The new concepts added to UML are derived from the ROOM which is also an object-oriented modeling technique optimized for complex, event-driven realtime system.

The fundamental modeling element of UML-RT is a capsule. A capsule represents independent flows of control in a system and communicates with other objects only by sending and receiving messages through interface objects called ports. A capsule may possess internal structures so that it is possible to describe complex systems in a hierarchical manner.

Capsules and connections between capsules' ports construct a structure model. The behavior of each capsule is described by a finite state machine. A capsule's state is changed by a message arrival at a capsule's port. A message can be thought of as an event in that a message has only one method to trigger actions. Thus, we use terms event and message interchangeably. In this paper, we use the UML-RT notations.

div.head: RoseRT and Run-Time Systems
div.p: RoseRT allows users to design an object-oriented real-time system by providing a visual modeling environment. It also allows them to automatically generate an executable program which is composed of application code, skeleton code, and run-time system service libraries. The core component of the RoseRT run-time system (RTS) is a controller object that dispatches messages to capsule instances. It takes the next message from a message queue and delivers it to the destination capsule instance by invoking the capsule's behavior described by a finite state machine. When there are multiple messages in the queue, it processes them according to their priorities. Thus, message priorities determine the priority of the action triggered by messages.

While UML-RT and RoseRT provide a visual modeling environment and a complete code generation tool for complex systems, they produce an application possessing unnecessary blocking sources. This makes it difficult to analyze the timing properties of the resultant system. In [9], Saksena et al. identified several sources of priority inversion that contributed to blocking time in applications designed with UML-RT. They proposed guidelines to avoid or minimize the unnecessary blocking. These blocking sources are (1) twolevel scheduling, (2) message passing, and (3) run-tocompletion. Our approach also exploits the guidelines to realize run-time service libraries and the underlying real-time operating system except the second guideline for reducing blocking time due to message passing. Note that our approach does not need ceiling priorities for message queues since there is no inter-thread message passing involved in our implementation model.

div.head: Proposed Mapping Methodology
div.p: In this section, we present our approach that can automatically generate multi-threaded implementations from any given real-time object-oriented design model. Figure 1 shows the overview of the proposed approach which is a three-step process: identifying (1) transactions, (2) logical threads, and then (3) physical threads. The first step derives transactions from a given design model. The second step groups mutually exclusive transactions, merges them into a task, and assigns each task a priority and preemption threshold. We refer to this task as a logical thread to differentiate it from a physical thread that actually comprises a final implementation. The final step merges logical threads into non-preemptive groups according to their priorities and preemption thresholds. Each non-preemptive group becomes a physical thread.

div.head: Design Models
div.p: A design model in our approach contains a set of external and internal events. Each external event initiates a transaction or multiple transactions. We denote transaction ~i by sequence of actions (Ai, Ai, ..., A i ; ) , All external events are periodic: We can convert a non-periodic event into a periodic one using its minimum inter-arrival time. We denote the period of transaction ~i by T(7-i).

The deadline of a transaction is the same as its period: This assumption is due to the limitation that end-to-end deadlines cannot be specified in UML-RT. Message priorities are determined not at design time but at implementation time: Our goal is to schedule all messages through our method without relying on fine-tuning of a design model. not impose serious limitations on the utility of the proposed approach since most systems in practice meet this assumption. For example, consider a robot command interpreter that accepts commands from an operator through buttons on the operator panel. If a command is "start a man- ual mode," it initiates a transaction which sets the robot to a manual mode. If the command is "start an automatic mode," it initiates another transaction which sets the robot to an automatic mode. We can see that these transactions start from the same active object and that they are mutually exclusive.

div.head: Deriving Transactions
div.p: The actions of a transaction may be blocked, due to the run-to-completion semantics, by a lower priority action that shares the same active object. As will be explained in Section 4, each active object has a mutex lock which helps maintain the run-to-completion semantics. Since the mutex lock makes use of the priority ceiling protocol, only the first action Af of ri may be blocked by a lower priority action. Therefore, transaction ~i has blocking time P(ri) as below. Until this step, a transaction has not been assigned a priority. Thus, this worst-case run-to-completion blocking time of a transaction can be computed after priority assignment at the next step.

div.head: Identifying Logical Threads
div.p: Identification of logical threads is a three-step process: for each logical thread, our approach identifies (1) its members, (2) priority, and (3) preemption threshold.

Grouping transactions: Identifying the members of a logical thread involves grouping mutually exclusive transactions. Transactions that share an active object as their first action can be grouped into a single logical thread. We denote a logical thread by Li = {rj}.
At run-time, a logical thread may have multiple periods, worst-case execution times, and run-to-completion blocking times since a logical thread may be a collection of transactions.

On the other hand, since interference for Li monotonically increases as C'(Lj)/T(Lj) increases, we assign C'(Li) and T ( L j ) values obtained from the transaction whose computation time to period ratio is the maximum.

div.head: Maximum preemption threshold assignment:
div.p: Our approach assigns a logical thread the maximum possible preemption threshold since a task with a higher preemption threshold experiences fewer context switches. We use the maximum preemption threshold assignment algorithm presented in [12]. This algorithm needs a different schedulability analysis slgorithm to take into account preemption thresholds. We also adopt the response time analysis algorithm in [12].

div.head: Identifying Physical Threads
div.p: Logical threads can be further aggregated into a non-preemptive group where every pair is mutually non-preemptive [ll, 121. Two logical threads Li and Lj are mutually non-preemptive if .ir(Li) 2 y(Lj) and n(Lj) 2 y(Li). With this relationship, we can easily construct non-preemptive groups of logical threads.
We can directly map a non-preemptive group into a physical thread. This can significantly reduce the number of threads, thus run-time context switching overhead and static memory resource demands.

div.head: Designing Tool for the Methodology
div.p: In this section, we describe how the RoseRT target run-time service library is designed and how its code generation feature is modified to support our approach.

div.head: Run-Time Systems
div.p: In RoseRT, an implementation-level thread has its own message processor called a controller. Each message contains a reference to its receiver capsule instance, which in turn has a reference to its controller.

Unlike RoseRT, our approach associates each message with a physical thread. To do so, we define a structure LogicalThread. It holds the priority and preemption threshold of a logical thread and a physical thread containing it. We extend the UML-RT message data structure (RTMessage class) to include LogicalThread and modify the arguments of message sending functions and a mechanism to find a target controller.

We change the controller such that it can dynamically process the priorities of received messages as in [ll]. Specifically, each controller should properly process received messages which have fixed priorities and preemption thresholds: (1) If a controller is processing a message, it should set its thread priority to the preemption threshold of the message. (2) If it is not processing any message, it should set the thread priority to the maximum of the priorities of messages in its message queue.

We use a mutex lock for each active object (RTActor class) to keep the run-to-completion semantics, We adopt the priority ceiling protocol [4]. We assign each mutex a ceiling priority equal to the maximum priority of messages sent to the active object which possesses the mutex. We modify the message dispatching routine (Controller: :dispatch()) so that it obtains a lock for the mutex of a receiver active object in advance before actually processing a message.

We also increase the message priority range of RoseRT since our approach tends to generate a large number of logical threads even for a system with a modest size. Note that RoseRT allows for only five priority levels. In an additional remark, we comment out -incarnateAllFixed() function call from RTMain: : entrypoint (1 function to prevent the association of all capsule instances with a main thread.

div.head: Code Generation
div.p: We need to patch the original RoseRT code generator only at three places. First, our approach synthesizes the body of RTMain: : initUpdateThreads0 so that it creates all the derived physical threads. Note that the RoseRT run-time system calls this function once during initialization to create all the user threads. The RoseRT code generator synthesizes the body of this function. Second, our code generator changes calls to the message sending functions to fill their extra arguments so that the attributes of logical threads can be determined via their arguments. Finally, our code generator sets values of ceiling priorities on mutexes of active objects which are for the run-to-completion semantics.
Since our approach needs only minimal changes to the original RoseRT code generator, it is straightforward to implement it in RoseRT.

div.head: Case Study: Soccer Robot
div.p: As a case study, we have designed a with UML-RT and fully synthesized its System soccer robot implement ation using the proposed-method. The robot soccer is a game in that two teams of autonomous robots compete with each other to get goals. There are many variants of robot soccer games. Each has a different rule and uses different types of robots. Interested readers are referred to [8] for more information. Each soccer robot contains a camera, two motors, a micro-controller, and a wireless communication module. In this case study, we have also realized two extra versions of the soccer robot using two other thread mappings and compared them with our approach.

div.head: Description of Soccer Robot
div.p: The soccer robot can receive two commands, stop and start, via a wireless communication device. Once the robot receives a start command, it searches a ball using information from the camera, calculates an optimal path to drive the ball, and then controls its motors to drive itself through the path. We used six capsule instances to model the robot control system. They are Communication, Vision, Location, Motor, Path-Tracker, and RobotControl capsule instances. Figure 2 shows the structure diagram of our soccer robot. Communication capsule instance receives a command from a wireless receiver and sends messages to RobotControl capsule instance. Vision capsule instance reads image data from the camera, distinguish visible objects, and send information on them to Location capsule instance. Location capsule instance receives messages about visible objects from Vision capsule instance, and calculates the locations of the ball, goals, and other robots. RobotControl capsule instance receives messages from Communication and Location capsule instances. It determines the action of the robot. PathTracker capsule instance receives the computed path information from RobotControl capsule instance. It then computes the desired speeds of its motors and sends them to Motor capsule instance. Finally, Motor capsule instance controls the motors. It also repeatedly sends PathTracker capsule instance a message containing the current location.

Table 1 shows the actions of each capsule instance and messages sent by these actions. It also shows the period and worst case execution time of each action. Note that RobotControl capsule instance can have either 100 ms or 200 ms as its period depending on its state. The colon (:) means a sub-state.

div.head: Comparison among Different Thread Mappings
div.p: In this case study, we have realized three different versions of the soccer robot using the proposed mapping and two other mappings. We compare these .three different implementations.

div.head: Single-Thread Mapping
div.p: This mapping groups all capsule instances into a single thread in that messages are processed in priority order. We can easily observe that this mapping produces a soccer robot that may not function correctly. As a specific example, consider a message from Motor capsule instance. It cannot be processed until a current transition completes its execution since transactions are executed non-preemptively in the single-threaded implementation. If the timeout interval of Motor capsule instance is smaller than the execution time of any other action in the system, Motor capsule may not be able to execute the action by the next timeout. To avoid this problem, we must re-design the application by breaking down all long actions into small fragments. However, this is not always possible.

div.head: Multi-Thread Mapping based on Capsule Instance
div.p: This mapping merges capsule instances into several groups and makes each of these groups a single thread.

It is used in RoseRT. To use this mapping, designers should determine how many threads are created and which capsule instances are merged together into a single thread. Table 2 shows the result of our design including the list of identified threads and their priorities. We grouped those capsule instances that had a connection between them expecting to reduce the overhead due to intra-thread message passing and context these logical threads.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: We have proposed a schedulability-aware software synthesis method that can automatically map real-time object-oriented design models to multi-threaded implementations. Our approach is composed of three steps: identifying (1) transactions, (2) logical threads, and then (3) physical threads. Our approach groups a set of mutually exclusive transactions into a logical thread, and then assigns each logical thread a priority such that the whole system can be schedulable. Since a logical thread may contain multiple transactions, it can possess multiple scheduling attributes such as periods, worst-case execution times, and blocking times. We provided a new schedulability analysis algorithm for this new task model. We adopted preemption threshold scheduling to reduce the amount of context switching overhead. Finally, our approach merges logical threads into non-preemptive groups according to the derived preemption thresholds and priorities. These non-preemptive groups become physical threads. This results in a significant reduction of the number of tasks, thus decrease in run-time context switching overhead and static memory resource demand.

In this paper, we also described in detail how RoseRT and its run-time system libraries should be extended to support our approach. The new RoseRT possesses (1) an extended message structure such that a message can contain the information of its designated logical thread, and (2) a new controller such that it can dynamically determine thread priorities according to the priorities and preemption thresholds of messages in its message queue.

We have performed a case study to demonstrate how the proposed method can be applied to a real-world problem. It shows the difficulty of task derivation problem and the utility of the automated synthesis of implement ation.

There are several future research directions. Currently, we are looking to extend the proposed approach to distributed system architectures. We are also attempting to finish up our implementation to integrate the proposed approach into RoseRT.
